chunk_findings.detail: A clean worktree plus a transient `git stash list` failure after a no-op `git stash push` now makes `_stash_away` raise `RuntimeError`, even though the correct contract is to return `""` because there was no work. `git stash push -u -m tag` exits 0 with “No local changes to save”; if `git stash list` then fails three times, `_stash_find_sure` returns `None`, and the fallback only recognizes the new entry if `refs/stash`’s top subject contains this operation’s tag. The old implementation returned `""` in this situation, so a no-change sync did not fail solely because the shared stash list was temporarily unreadable.

chunk_findings.detail: The new no-op detection searches `git`'s human-readable output for `"no local changes"`. Since a successful `git stash push -u -m tag` prints `Saved working directory and index state On <branch>: tag`, any `tag` containing `"no local changes"` makes `_stash_away(tree, "no local changes")` return `""` even though a stash was actually created. The caller will proceed as if the tree was clean and never apply that stash, orphaning the user's work. The helper's contract places no restriction on `tag`, so this is a regression from the previous lookup-by-tag behavior.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_stash_away

chunk_findings.detail: The retry predicate checks the substring `"stash failed"` anywhere in `r.err`/`r.out`, not just Git’s specific transient `fatal: stash failed` diagnostic. Git error output can contain arbitrary user-controlled file paths. For example, a tracked file named `stash failed` that conflicts during `git merge --no-edit <source>` produces `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in stash failed`; this is misclassified as a transient stash failure, so the function sleeps and re-runs `git merge` while `MERGE_HEAD` already exists. The result returned is then the second invocation’s `fatal: You have not concluded your merge` instead of Git’s actual conflict details. Match only the dedicated `fatal: stash failed` line, not any occurrence of the words.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py:_merge_retrying_stash

chunk_findings.detail: The test starts the lock-release timer before calling `W.merge`, but nothing guarantees `W.merge` reaches the first `git stash create` attempt before the held lock expires. Under a slow/loaded environment where `W.merge` spends more than 0.5s in setup before the first merge attempt, the lock is already gone, no `fatal: stash failed` occurs, and the merge succeeds on the first try; the test then passes even if `_merge_retrying_stash` has no retry logic at all. The 3s variant at line 55 has the same race. This makes the regression test nondeterministic and unable to distinguish a retried transient failure from a plain successful merge.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_merge_stash_retry.py:43 (and :55)

chunk_findings.detail: After `git stash push -u -m tag` succeeds with local changes, `_stash_away` treats any non-None `_stash_find_sure` result as authoritative. But `_stash_find_sure` returns `("", "")` whenever `git stash list` itself succeeds while the new entry is merely absent at that instant; that can happen in the shared-stash race this change is meant to handle. Concrete interleaving: session A pushes tagA and creates SHA_A. Session B is in `_drop` with a stale `stash@{n}` that now points at SHA_A; B runs `git stash drop` and gets SHA_A, but before B’s new `git stash store` puts it back, A runs `_stash_find_sure`: `git stash list` exits 0 and has no SHA_A, so `_stash_away` returns `""`. B then stores SHA_A back, but A already believes there was no local work and will not apply that stash after the sync; the user’s uncommitted work is left hidden in the stash. “List succeeded and no entry shown” is not proof that `git stash push` saved nothing, so the data-loss race remains open.

It never verifies that the stranger's stash entry still exists after the failed `stash store`. An implementation could lose the stranger's entry and still return exactly that incomplete message containing the SHA; the regression would pass even though the data-loss bug this fix is supposed to prevent is still present. chunk_findings.detail: The retry trigger is `"stash failed" in f"{r.err} {r.out}"`, so it matches any occurrence of that phrase, not the specific transient `fatal: stash failed` marker. If a merge conflicts on a path named `stash failed`, `git merge --no-edit <base>` returns nonzero with output like `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in stash failed`; the function sees the substring, sleeps, and runs `git merge` again. The first conflict has now created `MERGE_HEAD`, so the retry fails with `fatal: You have not concluded your merge`, and this second error is returned instead of the real conflict report. A genuine merge conflict is therefore misclassified and its output hidden.

chunk_findings.detail: The no-op check was anchored for `git stash push` output, but the actual stash-entry lookup still uses an unanchored substring (`if tag in subject`). Since the helper’s contract places no restriction on `tag`, `tag = "line1\nline2"` on a dirty tree makes `git stash push -u -m` succeed and create a stash whose `%gs` first line is only `On <branch>: line1`; the full tag is not in that subject, so `_stash_find` returns `("", "")` and `_stash_away` returns `""`. The command then proceeds as if the tree were clean, never applies that stash, and emits no restore note, leaving the user’s uncommitted work hidden in `refs/stash`. The new `startswith("no local changes")` special case does not catch this, because the offending tag is not the no-op message and the list lookup still has no anchored/exact match.

chunk_findings.detail: The exact-whole-line sentinel is still fooled by a path whose name is exactly `fatal: stash failed`. In `git merge`, a dirty or untracked file by that name is printed alone on an indented line before `Aborting`, e.g. `\tfatal: stash failed`; `ln.strip()` turns that into the sentinel, so `_stash_failed()` returns true for a normal "local changes would be overwritten" merge blocker. `_merge_retrying_stash()` then sleeps and re-runs the merge, and after four attempts returns the `git could not save the uncommitted state`/index-lock explanation even though no stash was attempted. A worktree containing `fatal: stash failed` with local changes that the merge would overwrite demonstrates this.

chunk_findings.detail: `_stash_failed` still tries to identify git's own error purely by an exact output line, but a conflicted path containing a newline can legitimately make `git merge` emit exactly `fatal: stash failed` as a whole line. For example, if the conflicting path is `a\nfatal: stash failed`, the first `git merge --no-edit <base>` prints the path literally, producing an output line `fatal: stash failed`. `_stash_failed` returns `True`, so `_merge_retrying_stash` sleeps and runs `git merge` again. The first conflict has already created `MERGE_HEAD`, so the retry fails with `fatal: You have not concluded your merge (MERGE_HEAD exists).` The original conflict result is lost and the merge is retried. The new test only covers a file named `stash failed`; this newline variant is a new false positive.

chunk_findings.detail: `_stash_back` calls `_stash_find_sure(tree, tag)` with the default `must_exist=False` immediately after successfully applying `sha`. That entry is known to still exist (`git stash apply` does not drop it), but under the shared-stash race this change targets, `git stash list` can succeed while the entry is transiently absent: for example, another worktree’s `_drop` has just mistakenly dropped this entry and has not yet stored it back. Because `must_exist` is false, `_stash_find_sure` returns `("", "")` on that first successful empty list, `_stash_back` then returns `""`, and when the other worktree stores the entry back, `ddflow sync --keep-local` has already reported success while the user’s stash entry remains in the stash. The same `_stash_find_sure(tree, sha)` calls in `_drop` after a failed `git stash drop` have the same flaw: an empty successful list is treated as “ours is gone” and can return success even though the entry will reappear. These known-to-exist paths should use `must_exist=True`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_stash_back and _drop

chunk_findings.detail: The regression uses the tag `"no local changes to save"` (lower-case n), but the actual Git “no work to stash” sentinel is `"No local changes to save"` (capital N). A case-sensitive implementation that mishandles the exact sentinel as a tag would still pass this test, because when a real stash is made with the lower-case tag, its successful output does not contain the uppercase sentinel. The boundary this test is meant to guard is the exact capital-N string; the test should pass `"No local changes to save"` to actually catch returning `""` after making a stash.

chunk_findings.detail: The newly added test does not actually answer the previous confirmed finding. The earlier defect was that `_stash_failed` treats an indented local-change-overwrite line such as `\tfatal: stash failed` as the sentinel after `strip()`. But this test never makes `git merge` emit that line: `test_a_stash_failure_from_a_briefly_held_index_lock_is_retried` and `test_a_stash_failure_that_never_clears_is_reported_with_its_cause` both require the merge path to use a pre-merge stash (the held `.git/index.lock` would otherwise produce an `Unable to create ... index.lock` error, not `fatal: stash failed`). With that pre-merge stash, the dirty file in this test is saved before the merge, so git logs `CONFLICT ... Merge conflict in fatal: stash failed`, not the exact sentinel line; the old `strip()` false positive would still return false here, leaving `_merge_retrying_stash` with no retry. Thus this test can pass with the original bug still present.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_merge_stash_retry.py:test_a_blocking_file_named_like_the_error_is_not_retried

chunk_findings.detail: The `_drop` success path trusts `re.search(r"\(([0-9a-f]{40,64})\)", r.out)` to learn which entry `git stash drop` actually dropped. On a normal Git configuration, `git stash drop` prints the abbreviated commit id from `git rev-parse --short` (default `core.abbrev` is 7, far fewer than 40 hex characters), so `got` is `None`. The very race this function is meant to handle is: `ref` goes stale and `git stash drop ref` drops a different worktree's stash entry. In that case this branch does `if not got ...: return ""`, so `_stash_back` reports success even though another session's stash entry was dropped and not stored back, and our own entry may remain. This is a concrete data-loss path in `ddflow sync --keep-local` and is not fixed by the new store/retry logic.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_drop

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test injects a `git stash store` failure, then asserts `theirs not in _git(wt, "stash", "list", "--format=%H")`. A correct fix that checks the store result and does not drop the stale ref when the store fails would leave the stranger's stash entry in `git stash list`; this assertion therefore fails on the safe behavior and only passes an implementation that still drops the stranger's entry after the store failure, merely reporting `DROP_INCOMPLETE`. That enshrines the exact data-loss path the change is supposed to fix: the stranger’s stash is removed from the stash stack even though `_drop` could not safely store it back. The assertion should expect `theirs` to remain in the list in this failure mode.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_sync_keep_local.py:test_a_stranger_entry_that_cannot_be_stored_back_is_reported

chunk_findings.detail: The new `MERGE_HEAD` guard does not protect the `--squash` path, and `_merge_retrying_stash` is also now used by `squash_merge` at `ddflow/infra/worktree.py:570`, where `args` can include `--squash`. `git merge --squash` deliberately does not record `$GIT_DIR/MERGE_HEAD`, so after a real squash conflict whose output carries the literal whole line `fatal: stash failed` (the accepted filename-with-newline case), `git rev-parse -q --verify MERGE_HEAD` fails and `_stash_failed` still returns `True`. The already-begun squash merge is then re-run, leaving the caller with the second attempt’s error instead of the original conflict, exactly what the guard was supposed to prevent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py:_stash_failed

chunk_findings.detail: The exact-line check still misclassifies a deterministic merge refusal as the transient index.lock stash failure. If the primary has an untracked file named `a\nfatal: stash failed` and a merge would overwrite it, `git merge` aborts before starting (or cleans up MERGE_HEAD), and the output contains `fatal: stash failed` as an exact line from the path. `_stash_failed` returns True, so `_merge_retrying_stash` sleeps STASH_RETRIES-1 times and retries a refusal that cannot become a transient stash failure. The MERGE_HEAD guard added for the previous conflict case does not help because no MERGE_HEAD survives this abort. The added tests only cover a plain `fatal: stash failed` file name without a newline and a MERGE_HEAD conflict simulation, so they do not catch this no-MERGE_HEAD newline case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py:_stash_failed

chunk_findings.detail:
The `all(ln.startswith(("error:", "fatal:")) for ln in lines)` check rejects the actual transient failure this change is meant to retry. With a held `.git/index.lock`, the pre-merge `git stash create` emits git's standard multi-line lock error:

```
fatal: Unable to create '.../.git/index.lock': File exists.

Another git process seems to be running in this repository, e.g.
an editor opened by 'git commit'. Please make sure all processes
are finished and then try again. If it still fails, a git process
may have crashed in this repository earlier:
remove the file manually to continue.
fatal: stash failed
```

The lines `Another git process seems...`, `an editor opened...`, and `remove the file...` do not start with `error:` or `fatal:`, so `all(...)` returns `False`. `_stash_failed` therefore returns `False`, `_merge_retrying_stash` never sleeps/retries, and the transient lock failure is still reported as the original merge failure. This directly defeats the fix for B-merge-stash-failed-transient.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/worktree.py:_stash_failed

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to guard against a blocking file named `fatal: stash failed`, but with the merge behavior this same file relies on elsewhere (`git merge` autostashing a dirty primary), the dirty tracked file is stashed rather than refused, and the output becomes a normal content-conflict message such as `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in fatal: stash failed`. That output never contains `fatal: stash failed` as an exact standalone line. As a result, an `_stash_failed` implementation that still had the exact-line-only misclassification would leave `pauses` empty and this test would still pass, so the test does not actually catch the regression it is named for.

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback path for “`git stash list` failed right after the push” uses `top.out` raw as the commit argument to `git log` and later returns it as the sha. `git rev-parse --verify -q refs/stash` normally emits a trailing newline, and this same patch explicitly `.strip()`s `W.git` output in this function, so the output is not guaranteed to be stripped. With `top.out` = `"<sha>\n"`, `git log -1 --format=%s "<sha>\n"` does not resolve, so this fallback fails and `_stash_away` raises even though the newly pushed entry could have been found. The raw value should be stripped before use.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/branchsync.py:_stash_away

chunk_findings.detail: `_stash_back` uses `None` as its success return (`why` is the reason string, and the previous code only touched it under `if why:`). The new first branch calls `why.startswith()` before that guard. On a successful restore, `why` is `None`, so this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'startswith'` immediately after the uncommitted work has been restored, aborting the sync. The guard order must be `if why: if why.startswith(...): ...` or normalize `why` to a string first.

chunk_findings.detail: The new “nothing was stashed” detection parses `git stash push`’s English text. In a non-English Git locale (for example `LC_ALL=fr_FR.UTF-8` or `LANG=de_DE.UTF-8`), a clean worktree prints that no-op message translated, so `startswith("no local changes")` is false. `_stash_find_sure` then finds no entry, `rev-parse refs/stash` fails if there is no pre-existing stash, and `_stash_away` raises `RuntimeError`, aborting the sync when there was nothing to stash. The previous code returned `""` for this case.

data.body:
Fixes bug B-merge-stash-retry-tests-patch-global-sleep: tests/test_merge_stash_retry.py (landed in fix-B-merge-stash-failed-transient) patches time.sleep GLOBALLY via monkeypatch.setattr(W.time, 'sleep', ...): any other thread's sleep during the test lands in the 'pauses' list, so under the full suite 3 tests fail (len(pauses)==4535, and 'not pauses' false). ci is red on main for it. Fix: replace the worktree module's time binding with a stub namespace instead of patching the shared time module. Found on fix-B-merge-stash-failed-transient.

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-B-merge-stash-retry-tests-patch-global-sleep --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed B-merge-stash-retry-tests-patch-global-sleep --regression-test <test>` first).

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test starts `neighbour` with `t.start()` but never ensures it has actually called `time.sleep` before `W.merge` runs. `threading.Thread.start()` returns as soon as the thread is started, not after the new thread is scheduled. In the interleaving where the OS does not schedule `neighbour` until after `W.merge` has already returned, the test passes even on the unfixed code that globally patches `time.sleep`, because no neighbour sleep ever lands in `pauses`. The test therefore does not reliably fail on the bug it is meant to catch.

data.title: tests/test_merge_stash_retry.py:test_other_threads_sleeping_do_not_count_as_the_merge_pauses

chunk_findings.detail: The `neighbour` thread is created as a non-daemon thread, but the `try/finally` that does `stop.set()` and `t.join()` only begins after `assert sleeping.wait(10)`. If that event wait times out (for example, the thread is not scheduled within 10 seconds under heavy CI load), the assert raises before `stop` is ever set, so the non-daemon `while not stop.is_set(): time.sleep(...)` loop runs forever. Python will then block forever joining that thread at interpreter shutdown after the failing test, turning a normal test failure into a hung suite.
